body:
Importance of Standardisation

The Harappan civilisation is distinguished by the use of similar artefacts and production standards across a large geographical area.

Pottery styles, seals, weights and brick proportions display considerable uniformity. This indicates that many settlements shared recognisable conventions for producing and using particular objects.

Standardisation means following common specifications or measures so that products or units remain comparable.

Such consistency could make exchange, construction and the manufacture of goods easier across different settlements.

Harappan Seals

Seals were among the most characteristic Harappan objects. Many were made of steatite, a relatively soft stone that could be carved and subsequently hardened by heating.

Harappan seals were commonly square, although other shapes also occurred. They frequently carried an animal motif together with signs belonging to the Harappan script.

Animal Motifs

Animals represented on seals include bulls, elephants, rhinoceroses, tigers and buffaloes. One of the most recognisable motifs is a one-horned animal conventionally called the unicorn.

The unicorn motif is a conventional description of an image. It does not establish that an actual one-horned animal of that form existed.

Although animal motifs probably carried meanings for the Harappans, their exact significance is not securely understood.

Seals and Sealings: The Difference

A seal is an object used to make an impression. A sealing is the impression left when the seal is pressed onto a soft material, often wet clay.

These objects may have helped identify goods and indicate whether a package had been opened.

How a Sealing Worked

  1. A bag or package containing goods was closed and tied.
  2. Wet clay was applied to the fastening or knot.
  3. A seal was pressed into the clay, leaving an impression.
  4. The clay hardened and preserved the impression.
  5. If the sealing remained intact when the goods arrived, it provided evidence that the fastening had not been disturbed.

The impression could also communicate information associated with the sender or the goods. Nevertheless, the precise information encoded by individual seal designs and inscriptions remains uncertain.

The Harappan Script

Many seals carried short inscriptions written in the Harappan script.

The script remains undeciphered. Consequently, scholars cannot reliably translate the inscriptions or establish with certainty what individual seal inscriptions stated.

Proposals that a particular seal recorded an owner's name, title or occupation are interpretations rather than confirmed translations.

This distinction matters when studying seals as commercial objects. Their probable practical use is supported by their physical form and distribution, but their complete written meaning remains unknown.

Standardised Weights

The Harappans used a carefully developed system of weights, which was important for comparing quantities of goods.

Many weights were made of chert, a hard siliceous stone. They were usually cubical and often had no numerical markings on their surfaces.

Binary and Decimal Relationships

Many lower denominations followed a binary progression, in which successive standard units doubled.

Examples include:

1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32.

Higher denominations also followed decimal relationships. The system therefore included different numerical patterns rather than depending entirely on one sequence.

Uses of Weights

Standard weights made it possible to compare quantities with greater consistency. Small weights may have been particularly useful for weighing beads, ornaments and other valuable materials.

Metal scale-pans have also been discovered, showing that weighing equipment formed part of Harappan material culture.

The existence of standardised weights does not establish that the Harappans used modern coins or a modern currency system.

Standardisation in Brick Production

Harappan construction also displayed standard proportions. Bricks at many settlements commonly followed the ratio:

Thickness : Width : Length = 1 : 2 : 4.

In other words, the width was approximately twice the thickness, and the length approximately 4 times the thickness.

This common proportion made bricks easier to combine in repeated construction patterns.

Brick production took place across different regions, so common proportions should not be confused with production in a single central factory.

Standardisation and Craft Organisation

The recurrence of similar weights, seals, bricks and pottery styles suggests that Harappan communities shared technical knowledge and common conventions.

Uniform specifications could support cooperation between different settlements and make manufactured objects more predictable in size, shape or function.

However, the material evidence alone cannot establish exactly which individuals or institutions supervised these standards. The political organisation responsible for maintaining them is not known with certainty.

Prelims focus

  • Harappan seals were commonly made of steatite.
  • The one-horned or unicorn motif is a familiar Harappan seal design.
  • Seal: the object used for stamping. Sealing: the resulting impression.
  • Standard weights were commonly cubical and made of chert.
  • Lower weight denominations frequently followed binary relationships.
  • Trap: The Harappan script remains undeciphered, and the standard brick proportion is 1 : 2 : 4 in the order thickness, width and length.

[NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 1, Bricks, Beads and Bones, pp. 6 and 15–16, sections 7 and 8; NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, Chapter 4, pp. 33, 36 and 40; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 2, Arts of the Indus Valley, pp. 11–12, section Seals.]

body:
Cotton Cultivation and Textile Production

The Harappans cultivated cotton and used textile fibres to produce cloth. Cotton was important because it supplied a raw material that could be spun into thread and woven into fabric.

Evidence of cotton cultivation in the wider northwestern subcontinent also predates the Mature Harappan cities. Mehrgarh is associated with early cotton cultivation.

Cotton is different from food crops such as wheat and barley because its principal importance in this context was as a source of textile fibre.

Spinning and Weaving

Spinning converts loose fibres into yarn or thread. Weaving produces cloth by interlacing threads.

Archaeologists have found spindle whorls made of materials such as terracotta and faience at Harappan settlements.

A spindle whorl is a small weighted object attached to a spindle. Its weight and rotation help twist fibres into thread.

The discovery of spindle whorls supports the conclusion that the Harappans practised spinning. Textile remains and impressions also show that woven materials were produced.

However, the precise organisation of textile production and the identities of all the people engaged in spinning and weaving are not fully known.

Physical Evidence of Cotton Cloth

Actual fragments of cotton cloth have been found at Mohenjodaro. Some were preserved in association with a silver vessel and copper objects.

Such finds are important because cotton and other organic materials usually decay over long periods. Contact with metal objects can sometimes help preserve traces or impressions of textiles.

Physical textile fragments provide a different kind of evidence from sculptures showing people wearing garments. Both are useful, but they should not be treated as identical.

Early Evidence of Dyed Cloth

A fragment of cotton cloth from Mohenjodaro has been reported as having been dyed red with madder.

Madder is a plant-derived source of red dye. Its use in colouring cloth is an important indication of knowledge of textile treatment and decoration.

This find is among the notable early examples of dyed cotton cloth associated with the Harappan world. It should not be described unconditionally as the earliest dyed fabric anywhere in the world, because other early textile traditions and finds must also be considered.

Mohenjodaro: surviving cotton textile fragments, including a reported example of cloth dyed red using madder.

Early Evidence Associated with Embroidered or Decorated Garments

A well-known stone figure from Mohenjodaro, conventionally called the Priest-King, is shown wearing a garment over one shoulder.

The garment carries a distinctive trefoil pattern. A trefoil consists of a decorative arrangement resembling 3 connected lobes or leaf-like forms.

The patterned garment has often been described in textbooks as embroidered. The sculpture provides early evidence of elaborate textile decoration, and embroidery is one possible way such designs could have been produced.

However, the carved pattern does not conclusively establish the precise textile technique. Embroidery, dyeing and other decorative methods must be distinguished from one another.

Most importantly, the sculpture is evidence for a depicted decorated garment, not a surviving piece of embroidered cloth.

Distinguishing the Evidence

EvidenceAssociated siteWhat it establishes
Cotton fragmentsMohenjodaroActual textile material was used
Reported madder-dyed cottonMohenjodaroEarly evidence associated with red textile dyeing
Spindle whorlsSeveral Harappan sitesKnowledge and practice of spinning
Trefoil-patterned garment on stone figureMohenjodaroDepiction of decorated clothing; embroidery is a possible interpretation

For objective questions, remember both the relevant discovery and the level of certainty attached to it. Evidence for cotton cloth is more direct than an inference about the exact method used to decorate a garment represented in stone.

Gujarat's Contribution to Harappan Agriculture and Crafts

Gujarat formed an important part of the Harappan cultural region. Its settlements combined local agricultural resources with specialised production of beads, shell objects, pottery and metal goods.

Lothal

Lothal was associated with bead manufacture, stone and metal crafts, and the handling of goods. The discovery of a bead workshop, unfinished products, tools and finished beads makes it a particularly important location for understanding craft specialisation.

The settlement also possessed a storehouse associated with seals and sealings.

Dholavira

Dholavira demonstrates the relationship between technical expertise and environmental adaptation. Its reservoirs and water-management facilities helped the settlement function in a dry landscape.

The site also yielded evidence of bead workshops and objects made from stone, copper, shell and other materials.

Nageshwar

Nageshwar was associated with the production of shell objects. Its coastal location provided access to marine shells that could be transformed into bangles, ladles and decorative pieces.

Other Gujarat Evidence

Gujarat's Harappan agricultural economy was not identical to that of the central Indus plains. Millets were important in parts of the region, while sites such as Khirsara have provided evidence for several other cultivated crops.

These findings show that Harappan settlements adapted agriculture and production activities to different local resources.

Key Site–Evidence Associations

DholaviraGujaratReservoirs, bead processing and specialised crafts
NageshwarGujaratShell-working centre
BalakotPakistanShell-working centre
KhirsaraGujaratEvidence of diverse cultivated crops

How Agriculture and Crafts Supported One Another

The Harappan economy depended upon the relationship between food production, access to resources and specialised manufacturing.

Farmers and herders supplied food and other useful products. Craftspersons transformed materials such as metal, stone, clay, shell and cotton into tools, vessels, ornaments and textiles.

Different settlements possessed different advantages. Some were close to agricultural land and water, others were near sources of valuable stones or marine shells, and still others developed substantial manufacturing activities.

The use of similar weights, seals and manufacturing conventions helped connect these activities across the wider Harappan region.

Prelims focus

  • Mohenjodaro yielded surviving cotton cloth, including a reported madder-dyed example.
  • The so-called Priest-King sculpture shows a trefoil-patterned garment.
  • Spindle whorls provide evidence of spinning.
  • Lothal and Dholavira were important Gujarat craft centres.
  • Nageshwar was associated with shell working.
  • Trap: A depiction of a decorated garment is not the same as the discovery of surviving embroidered fabric.

[NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, Chapter 4, In the Earliest Cities, pp. 36–40; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 2, Arts of the Indus Valley, pp. 9 and 14–15; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 6, pp. 96–101; Ruth Barnes, Indian Block-Printed Textiles in Egypt: The Newberry Collection in the Ashmolean Museum, 1997, section History of Research, Ashmolean Museum online edition, accessed 17 November 2026; Harappa.com, Jane McIntosh and Richard H. Meadow, What Did the Indus People Wear and What Material Were Their Clothes Made Of?, accessed 17 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Dholavira: a Harappan City, Brief Synthesis, accessed 17 November 2026.]
